posts.hook: The longer you wait to send an invoice, the longer you wait to get paid.
posts.why: An invoice that shows up a week after the job feels optional. One that arrives the same day feels like part of the job.
steps: Send the invoice the same day, or before you leave the job if you can.
Put the due date and how to pay right at the top, in plain words.
Make paying a one step thing, like a link or a card tap, so there's no excuse to wait.
posts.take: Fast invoices get paid fast. Cash flow loves a quick sender.

posts.hook: Mixing business and personal money is the fastest way to lose track of both.
posts.why: When everything runs through one account, you can't see what the business really earns, and tax time turns into a scavenger hunt.
steps: Open a separate checking account just for the business.
Pay yourself a set amount on a set day and leave the rest in the business.
Ask your accountant what to set aside for taxes, since the right answer depends on your setup.
posts.take: Clean accounts give you clean answers. Check the details with an accountant.

posts.hook: Your website has about 3 seconds to prove it's worth waiting for.
posts.why: Google's research found 53% of mobile visitors leave a site that takes longer than 3 seconds to load. Not annoyed. Gone.
posts.src: Think with Google, via Marketing Dive
steps: Open your site on your phone using cellular data, not WiFi, and count to 3. Not ready? That's a speed problem.
Run your homepage through Google's free PageSpeed Insights and read the mobile results first.
Shrink your biggest photos with a free tool like TinyPNG. They'll look the same and load faster.
posts.take: A faster site means more of the people you already paid to attract actually stick around.

posts.hook: Answer the phone like the caller is already a customer.

Say your business name and your own name, then ask how you can help.
If you can't answer, text back right away and say when you'll call.

posts.hook: Most quotes die in the customer's inbox. A simple nudge brings them back.
posts.why: Customers get busy and forget, even when they liked your price. A friendly reminder is good service, not pushiness.
steps: Send the quote with a clear next step, like “Reply yes and I'll hold a date for you.”
Follow up in two or three days with a short, friendly message.
If you hear nothing, check once more in a week and then let it go politely.
posts.take: A polite nudge wins jobs that silence would have lost.

posts.hook: Know the lowest price you can take before you quote any job.
posts.why: Quoting on the spot without knowing your floor is how good jobs end up losing money.
steps: Add up your costs for the job, including your time, materials, and driving.
Add the profit you need so the business stays healthy.
Write that number down and never go below it, no matter how nice the customer is.
posts.take: A job that loses money isn't a win. It's a favor.
